analysis.one_liner: Extends background checks to gun shows, sets a handgun waiting period, and tightens youth and trafficking rules.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by Sen. Charles Schumer with 10 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would close the gun-show loophole by requiring background checks on all sales at gun shows, force show promoters to register and keep vendor records, and add a mandatory 72-hour minimum wait for handgun purchases with a longer background-check window. It would raise the minimum age for handgun purchases to 21, require dealers to include a lock or safety device with every gun sold, limit buyers to one handgun per 30 days, ban imports of large-capacity ammunition magazines, boost penalties for traffickers, and fund more gun prosecutions and dealer inspections.
analysis.who_benefits: People in communities affected by gun violence, since the bill's stated aim is to keep guns away from criminals, traffickers, and people under 21. Police get more time for background checks, better tracing of crime guns, and new funding for enforcement projects.

how_it_helps.text: Extends Brady criminal background checks to every firearm transfer at gun shows, which the bill's findings describe as places where criminals can buy guns anonymously without checks or tracing records.

Sets a mandatory 72-hour minimum wait for handgun and semiautomatic assault weapon purchases and extends the background-check window from three to five business days so investigators have more time to finish a check.

Raises the minimum age to buy a handgun to 21 and bars under-21s from semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, with exemptions for farming, target practice, hunting, employment, and self-defense at home.
Requires licensed dealers to provide a secure gun storage device or lock with every firearm sold and penalizes adults whose loaded firearms, accessible to children, cause death or serious injury.
Limits any buyer to one handgun per 30 days and increases penalties for gun traffickers, false dealer records, and dealers who fail compliance inspections.
Funds intensive gun-prosecution projects and expands the Youth Crime Gun Interdiction Initiative to 75 city and county police agencies to trace the sources of crime guns.

analysis.who_pays: Licensed gun dealers, gun show promoters, and firearms manufacturers, who would face registration fees, new recordkeeping, warrantless compliance inspections, mandatory safety-device sales, a one-handgun-per-month limit, and an import ban on large-capacity magazines. Some law-abiding buyers would also face longer waits and purchase limits.

drawbacks.text: The one-handgun-per-30-days rule would restrict how quickly a lawful buyer can acquire multiple handguns, including collectors and people assembling a personal collection, though the bill carves out exemptions for family transfers, pawn redemptions, security companies, and lost or stolen replacements.

The bill lets the Treasury inspect gun show venues and promoter records during business hours without a showing of reasonable cause or a warrant, and requires show promoters to register, pay fees, and file vendor lists 72 hours in advance, a compliance burden that falls hardest on small operators.

The mandatory 72-hour handgun waiting period would delay purchases even by people who pass a fast background check, though the bill allows an immediate exception for people who obtain a written certification from local law enforcement that they face a threat to their life.
The bill adds enhanced criminal penalties for youth possession and makes juvenile adjudications count as firearm prohibitions, extending punishment rather than only adding regulatory checks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core aim, background checks at gun shows and a longer window for checks to finish, addresses a documented gap in the existing law and carries real benefits for public safety. The costs fall mostly on dealers and promoters in the form of paperwork, fees, and inspections, and on a minority of buyers in the form of delays and the one-gun-per-month cap. The warrantless inspection authority and purchase limit are the provisions most open to fair objection, since they burden lawful conduct along with trafficking.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it was sent the day it was introduced, and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a Senate floor vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Charles Schumer introduced the bill on May 11, 1999, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee that same day.
Ten Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The committee took no further action on the bill, and its only recorded action in the entire 106th Congress is the introduction and referral.
The bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms dealers, gun show promoters, and gun manufacturers are better off, because none of the new background-check, registration, inspection, or import restrictions took effect. Buyers who would have faced longer waits or the one-handgun-per-month cap also kept current rules.

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Youth Gun Crime Enforcement Act in the Senate.

for.name: 10 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Feinstein, Kennedy, Durbin, Mikulski, Levin, Boxer, Torricelli, Lautenberg, Reed, and Kerry.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Majority leadership of the Senate Judiciary Committee, the committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after referring it, leaving it to die at the end of the 106th Congress.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed extending background checks to gun shows and new dealer regulations during the 1999 gun-legislation debate.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the Republican majority that controlled the Senate agenda and the Judiciary Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Firearms dealers and gun show promoters
industries.note: The bill would require show promoters to register, pay fees, file vendor lists, and keep ledgers, and would route every gun-show sale through a licensed dealer running a background check. Their business model of high-volume, lightly recorded sales is exactly what the bill targets.

The bill bans imports of large-capacity ammunition magazines, requires a safety device with every gun sold, adds inspections and storage rules, and raises penalties for recordkeeping violations. Gunsmiths would also need a separate, fee-based license.
Buyers of explosive materials would need federal background checks, and license applicants would submit fingerprints and photographs with fees up to $300, adding cost and friction to the trade.
